name: Noakhali dialect of Bengali, 'ND'
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Morshed, Abul Kalam Manzur. 1972 [UBC cIRcle / Glottolog: 1975]. The phonological, morphological and syntactical patterns of standard colloquial Bengali and the Noakhali dialect. MA thesis, Department of Linguistics, University of British Columbia, xii+159 pp. DOI 10.14288/1.0093434. Corroborated by Haldar, Gopal. 1929. A Brief Phonetic Sketch of the Noakhali Dialect of South-Eastern Bengali. Journal of the Department of Letters (University of Calcutta) XIX: 1-40, 'Stress-Accent' secs. 50 and 58, pp. 28-29.
catalog_locator: Morshed 1972, ch. 2, sec. 2.5 'Suprasegmental features', subsecs. 2.51-2.53, thesis pp. 49-50. Haldar 1929, 'Stress-Accent' secs. 50 and 58, pp. 28-29
catalog_quote: Stress is not phonemic in either SCB and ND as it does not exist with contrasts on the position of intensity. It may be said that its position is automatic and does not have any semantic role. Due to its non-phonemicity, there are no contrasting levels of stress. It is so non-significant that the presence or absence or position does not alter the sense of any morphemes (Chatterjee, 1921-19). SCB and ND have emphatic stress which is used to give emphasis and contrast (Ferguson and Chowdhury, 1960-25). ... 2.52. Both in SCB and ND stress is predictable mostly for the inflected morphemes where it is always placed on the initial syllable. The following examples will show the initial stress system of the language. ... ND [ˈdʒɔr oiše] I got fever; [ˈadʒ ki kirum] what shall I do to-day?; [ˈhe balai kam kɔre] He got a good job. 2.53. Though word stress is always subsidiary to sentence-stress, there are few exceptions to this rule. Chatterjee (1921-19) shows that conjunctions, particles, auxiliaries in compound verbs do not receive any stress. If any noun follows an adjective it loses the stress, which falls on the adjective. The initial stressing system of the language has caused umlaut and vowel harmony.
world_status: statement found in an open source

SCB and ND have emphatic stress which is used…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress in the Noakhali dialect (ND) is non-contrastive and automatic: it falls on the initial syllable of the word, and at phrase level on the initial syllable of the first content word of the sense-group, all other words losing their stress. Morshed's ND examples mark the first syllable of the utterance: ['dʒɔr oiʃe] 'I got fever', ['adʒ ki kirum] 'what shall I do to-day?', ['he balai kam kɔre] 'he got a good job'. Haldar 1929 (pp. 28-29) independently reaches the same conclusion for Noakhali ('the initial word-stress prevails just as in the Standard Colloquial speech'), with word-level evidence from the lengthening of initial vowels and the elision or shortening of the vowel of the following syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described. Morshed: 'there are no contrasting levels of stress'; only an emphatic stress (tenser consonants, lengthened vowels over a syllable) exists besides the automatic initial stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Morshed: conjunctions, particles and the auxiliary of compound verbs are unstressed; a noun following an adjective loses its stress to the adjective (both after Chatterji 1921). Haldar 1929: in Persian/Arabic loans 'the stress is thrown back' (i.e. still initial, cf. LSI V-1); his sec. 58 notes 'puzzles' -- extended name forms like [ɦasoinna] 'Hasan', [khitta] 'Kshitisa' where the dialect resists the vowel modification that strong initial stress produces in Standard Bengali -- but he still holds initial stress to prevail in connected speech.
new_statements.domain_note: Both sources treat stress as primarily a sentence/sense-group phenomenon with word stress 'subsidiary to sentence-stress'; Morshed's ND examples are short sentences, not isolated citation forms, and his statement is framed as holding for both Standard Colloquial Bengali (SCB) and ND, drawing the rule partly from Chatterji 1921 on SCB. Haldar's 1929 evidence (initial-vowel lengthening, post-tonic vowel loss in words like ['suiʈka], ['petni]) is word-level. Morshed's ND is Dialect (B), the central (Maijdi) Noakhali variety, from two educated informants aged 27-29 resident in Vancouver.
new_statements.identity_note: Morshed 1972 explicitly describes Dialect (B), the central / Maijdi variety of Noakhali District (informants from 'central part of Noakhali', pp. 17-18); Glottolog's language code for this reference is 'Maijdi Noakhali = Central Noakhali = Noakhali', i.e. the language-level entry noak1234 itself, not one of its dialect children (feni1234 Feni, hati1234 Hatia, etc.). Haldar 1929 describes the mainland Noakhali patois as a whole, distinguishing it from Chittagongese (chit1275), Sandip and the Chandpur/Dacca variety, and his stress section also applies to the district dialect generally. Rashel 2011 covers the Chatkhil (western) sub-dialect and is silent on stress.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the very source the catalog record and the existing statement were built from; the re-read confirms the quoted sentences, the page numbers (thesis pp. 49-50 = pp. 63-64) and the reading 'fixed: initial syllable' = catalog initial stress. Nothing in the thesis contradicts it. The statement is explicitly about both SCB and ND ('Both in SCB and ND'), so the catalog's ND entry rests on a joint statement rather than an ND-only one.0093434/1 endpoint, and both returned the 4.9 kB 'unusual activity' block page; the copy read is the archive.org user-upload of the same UBC PDF already held by the project ( records both).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and automatic in both Standard Colloquial Bengali and the Noakhali dialect; it falls on the initial syllable (p. 50: 'always placed on the initial syllable', 'the initial stress system of the language'), and the same page says this initial stressing has caused umlaut and vowel harmony. Word stress is subordinate to sentence stress. Examples given for ND (p. 50): [ˈdʒɔr oiše] 'I got fever', [ˈadʒ ki kirum] 'what shall I do to-day?', [ˈhe balai kam kɔre] 'He got a good job'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress. Sec. 2.51 adds that there are no contrasting levels of stress, and that SCB and ND have an emphatic stress used for emphasis and contrast, realised by tenser consonant articulation and vowel lengthening spreading over a syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Sec. 2.53 (p. 50): word stress is always subsidiary to sentence stress; conjunctions, particles and auxiliaries in compound verbs receive no stress (citing Chatterjee 1921: 19); a noun following an adjective loses its stress, which falls on the adjective. The p. 50 examples show stress on the first word of the phrase only.
new_statements.identity_note: Morshed's ND corpus comes from two informants (thesis pp. 17-18) 'from the same region (central part of Noakhali, Dialect B)', i.e. the central mainland Maijdi area of Noakhali district, checked against three sailors from the dialect area; the thesis distinguishes three Noakhali sub-dialects (Feni area, Maijdi area, Hatia islands; Fig. 1 and Map 2). The stress statement itself is made jointly for SCB and ND and is partly cited from Chatterjee 1921 (on SCB) and Ferguson and Chowdhury 1960, so it is not an ND-specific finding.

tone_statements.citation: হুমায়ুন, রাজীব [Humayun, Rajib]. 1982 [বর্ষা ১৩৮৯ issue]. সন্দ্বীপের আঞ্চলিক ভাষা : ধ্বনিতত্ত্ব ও রূপ-ধ্বনিতত্ত্ব [The regional speech of Sandwip: phonology and morphophonology]. সাহিত্য পত্রিকা (Sahitya Patrika, Department of Bengali, University of Dhaka) 25(2): 63-85. doi:10.62328/sp.v25i2.3.
tone_statements.quote: [p. 65] স্বন (tone) : অবরোহী /ˋ/ আরোহী /ˊ/ [...] সন্দ্বীপীর ধ্বনিমূল তালিকার সাথে প্রমিত (standard) কথ্যবাঙলার ধ্বনিমূল তালিকা মিলিয়ে দেখলে কিছু গুরুত্বপূর্ণ পার্থক্য চোখে পড়বে। [...] এ' তালিকায় সবচাইতে উল্লেখযোগ্য হল, স্বনের উপস্থিতি। ঐতিহাসিক ভাষাবিজ্ঞানের দৃষ্টিকোণ থেকে বলা যায় সন্দ্বীপীতে (হয়তোবা আরো কিছু আঞ্চলিক বাঙলায়) স্বন এসেছে মূলতঃ ক্ষতিপূরণ হিসেবে। ধরা যাক, কথ্যবাঙলা থেকে [p. 66] সন্দ্বীপী 'শহর' শব্দটি ধার করল। সন্দ্বীপীতে শব্দের মধ্য অবস্থানে 'হ' ব্যবহারের প্রবণতা কম। ফলে 'শহর' শব্দটি 'শর' হিসেবে ব্যবহৃত হবার কথা। কিন্তু 'হ'র ক্ষতিপূরণ হিসেবে 'শ'-এর 'অ'র সাথে আরোহী-স্বন যুক্ত হবে। ফলে উচ্চারণ দাঁড়াবে /শ́র/ (ʃɔ́r) অর্থাৎ 'অ' কে সামান্য উপরের দিকে টেনে পরে নীচের দিকে অতি সামান্য বাঁকিয়ে উচ্চারণ করা হবে। কিন্তু এও সত্য, 'স্বনিতভাষা'-সমূহের অধিকাংশ বৈশিষ্ট্য সন্দ্বীপীতে পাওয়া যাবে না (১.৫ দেখুন)। [p. 72] ১.২.৪. স্বন : নিম্নোক্ত শিরোণামায় স্বনসমূহের মাঝে বৈপরীত্য দেখানো হয়েছে : ১. অবরোহী বনাম আরোহী ২. অনুপস্থিতি বনাম অবরোহী এবং ৩. অনুপস্থিতি বনাম আরোহী স্বন
tone_statements.translation: [p. 65] Tone: falling /ˋ/, rising /ˊ/ [...] If the phoneme inventory of Sandwipi is set beside that of standard colloquial Bangla, some important differences strike the eye. [...] The most noteworthy thing in this inventory is the presence of tone. From the standpoint of historical linguistics one may say that in Sandwipi (and perhaps in some other regional Bangla) tone has come in essentially as compensation. Suppose [p. 66] Sandwipi borrowed the word শহর 'town' from colloquial Bangla. In Sandwipi h is rarely used word-medially, so শহর ought to be used as শর. But as compensation for the h a rising tone is joined to the ɔ of শ, so the pronunciation becomes /ʃɔ́r/, i.e. the ɔ is pulled slightly upward and then bent very slightly downward. But it is also true that most of the characteristics of 'tone languages' will not be found in Sandwipi (see 1.5). [p. 72] 1.2.4 Tone: contrasts among the tones are shown under the following heads: 1. falling versus rising, 2. absence versus falling, and 3. absence versus rising tone.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 1.1 phoneme inventory 'স্বন (tone)' p. 65 and discussion pp. 65-66; sec. 1.2.4 'স্বন' (tone contrasts, minimal pairs) pp. 72-73; sec. 1.2.5 intonation p. 73
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Two marked lexical tones (falling, rising) contrasting with toneless syllables on the word's (first) vowel, i.e. a three-way privative contrast; tones are reflexes of lost h/aspiration (compensatory), so functional load is limited; intonation handled separately with 4 pitch levels.

sources.note: Pronunciation notes for the South-Eastern dialect, explicitly 'based on Mr. Pargiter's work' on Chittagong with Noakhali/Hatia additions: 'In words of several syllables, especially those borrowed from Persian or Arabic, the accent is thrown back as far as possible, and the following syllables are lightened. sources.quote: [p. 65] স্বন (tone) : অবরোহী /ˋ/ আরোহী /ˊ/ [...] সন্দ্বীপীর ধ্বনিমূল তালিকার সাথে প্রমিত (standard) কথ্যবাঙলার ধ্বনিমূল তালিকা মিলিয়ে দেখলে কিছু গুরুত্বপূর্ণ পার্থক্য চোখে পড়বে। [...] এ' তালিকায় সবচাইতে উল্লেখযোগ্য হল, স্বনের উপস্থিতি। ঐতিহাসিক ভাষাবিজ্ঞানের দৃষ্টিকোণ থেকে বলা যায় সন্দ্বীপীতে (হয়তোবা আরো কিছু আঞ্চলিক বাঙলায়) স্বন এসেছে মূলতঃ ক্ষতিপূরণ হিসেবে। ধরা যাক, কথ্যবাঙলা থেকে [p. 66] সন্দ্বীপী 'শহর' শব্দটি ধার করল। সন্দ্বীপীতে শব্দের মধ্য অবস্থানে 'হ' ব্যবহারের প্রবণতা কম। ফলে 'শহর' শব্দটি 'শর' হিসেবে ব্যবহৃত হবার কথা। কিন্তু 'হ'র ক্ষতিপূরণ হিসেবে 'শ'-এর 'অ'র সাথে আরোহী-স্বন যুক্ত হবে। ফলে উচ্চারণ দাঁড়াবে /শ́র/ (ʃɔ́r) অর্থাৎ 'অ' কে সামান্য উপরের দিকে টেনে পরে নীচের দিকে অতি সামান্য বাঁকিয়ে উচ্চারণ করা হবে। কিন্তু এও সত্য, 'স্বনিতভাষা'-সমূহের অধিকাংশ বৈশিষ্ট্য সন্দ্বীপীতে পাওয়া যাবে না (১.৫ দেখুন)। [p. 72] ১.২.৪. স্বন : নিম্নোক্ত শিরোণামায় স্বনসমূহের মাঝে বৈপরীত্য দেখানো হয়েছে : ১. অবরোহী বনাম আরোহী ২. অনুপস্থিতি বনাম অবরোহী এবং ৩. অনুপস্থিতি বনাম আরোহী স্বন

tone.translation: [p. 65] Tone: falling /ˋ/, rising /ˊ/ [...] If the phoneme inventory of Sandwipi is set beside that of standard colloquial Bangla, some important differences strike the eye. [...] The most noteworthy thing in this inventory is the presence of tone. From the standpoint of historical linguistics one may say that in Sandwipi (and perhaps in some other regional Bangla) tone has come in essentially as compensation. Suppose [p. 66] Sandwipi borrowed the word শহর 'town' from colloquial Bangla. In Sandwipi h is rarely used word-medially, so শহর ought to be used as শর. But as compensation for the h a rising tone is joined to the ɔ of শ, so the pronunciation becomes /ʃɔ́r/, i.e. the ɔ is pulled slightly upward and then bent very slightly downward. But it is also true that most of the characteristics of 'tone languages' will not be found in Sandwipi (see 1.5). [p. 72] 1.2.4 Tone: contrasts among the tones are shown under the following heads: 1. falling versus rising, 2. absence versus falling, and 3. absence versus rising tone.
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: Two marked lexical tones (falling, rising) contrasting with toneless syllables on the word's (first) vowel, i.e. a three-way privative contrast; tones are reflexes of lost h/aspiration (compensatory), so functional load is limited; intonation handled separately with 4 pitch levels.

sources.note: Describes another variety (Glottolog vang1242). Snippet (as quoted in the Wikipedia footnote, p. 102): 'Glottalization is often connected with tone and in the East Bengali cases seem to be related to the evolution of tone from the voiced aspirates.' The citing Wikipedia note paraphrases: the voiced aspirated series is missing in the Eastern Bengali of Sylhet, Barak Valley, Cumilla, Tripura, Noakhali and Chittagong, 'where it is replaced by tone, as in Punjabi'. A secondary comparative statement, not a description of the Noakhali tone system.
